title: Recent advances in functionalized electrospun nanofibers for biomedical and therapeutic applications: A comprehensive review

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Recent advances in functionalized electrospun nanofibers for biomedical and therapeutic applications: A comprehensive review》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p1040】Nanotechnology has rapidly evolved into a highly impactful research field with significant potential for advancements in healthcare and biomedical sciences. In particular, polymeric micro- and nanofibers (NFs) have attracted increasing attention in biomedical engineering as key building blocks for devices and functional biomaterials [1]. Among various fabrication techniques, electrospinning (ES) has become a leading method for nanofiber production due to its wide applicability in pharmaceuticals and medicine. Through electrostatic interactions, a viscoelastic polymer solution is drawn into continuous fibers, enabling the fabrication of nanoscale structures in a simple and versatile manner [2]. ES is widely valued for its operational simplicity, scalability, and the ability to finely tune fiber diameter, composition, and orientation [3]. ES permits the fabrication of fibers of diameters ranging from the micrometer-to-nanometer scale, utilizing a wide spectrum of materials, including polymers of natural or synthetic origin, ceramics, small molecules, and hybrid systems [2]. In addition, ES allows the fabrication of specialized structures, including porous, hollow, and core-sheath fibers. These structures could be further functionalized by incorporating bioactive agents or nanoparticles (NPs) during or after spinning. Beyond single fibers, more complex architectures, including aligned, layered, and three-dimensional (3D) assemblies, can be achieved through controlled deposition strategies [2], [3], [4], [5]. Owing to these versatile features, electrospun nanofibers (ESNFs) have been widely applied in filtration, catalysis, environmental protection, energy systems, and functional textiles. In biomedical applications, they are particularly important for tissue engineering (TE), wound healing, drug delivery (DD), and regenerative therapies [2].

【Introduction · p1045】The development of ES spans several centuries. Early observations of electrostatic effects on liquids were reported by William Gilbert in 1600 [6], [7]. In the 18th century, Stephen Gray and Abbe Nollet described electrostatically driven fluid jets and electrospraying phenomena. A major step toward modern ES occurred in 1902 with Cooley and Morton, who developed early device concepts [7]. In 1914, John Zeleny analyzed fluid behavior under the influence of electric fields using mathematical models. Geoffrey Taylor, in work conducted between 1964 and 1969, provided the theoretical basis for jet formation by describing the “Taylor cone.” Despite these advances, the field saw limited progress for several decades until its revival in 1990 by Darrell Reneker and Gregory Rutledge, who demonstrated the polymer-based fiber production and significantly expanded its application potential [7], [8]. An illustrative overview of this historical development is shown in Fig. 1.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Recent advances in functionalized electrospun nanofibers for biomedical and therapeutic applications: A comprehensive review》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Functionalization methods of electrospun nanofibers · p1120】Modifying or functionalizing the surface of ESNFs is a widely used strategy to enhance key surface features like wettability, surface charge, and roughness, thereby improving their performance in biomedical applications. The integration of biological molecules including nutrients, proteins, growth factors, and other bioactive or biomimetic materials into or onto nanofiber matrices, can create a favorable microenvironment that facilitates stem cell adhesion, differentiation, and proliferation. This, in turn, enhances the bioactivity of the platforms and broadens their applicability in regenerative medicine and related fields [128], [129], [130]. Surface modification strategies are generally categorized into two main approaches: (i) physical methods, such as adsorption or non-covalent functionalization, and (ii) chemical methods, including plasma treatment and graft polymerization [128], [129]. Physical modification is often preferred for its simplicity and for preserving the intrinsic structure of NFs, as it does not involve chemical reactions that may alter bulk properties [130]. This approach relies on weak, non-covalent interactions (e.g., van der Waals interactions, electrostatic forces, hydrogen bonding, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic effects) [131]. However, these interactions are typically less stable over time, which may limit long-term functionality. In contrast, chemical modification involves covalent bonding and permanent alteration of the nanofiber surface through the addition or activation of functional groups, thereby enhancing surface hydrophilicity and enabling stable biomolecule immobilization. This process is typically initiated by activating reactive groups on the nanofiber surface, such as -COOH, -NH2, or -OH, followed by their reaction with bioactive molecules to form stable covalent linkages [128], [132]. Because these bonds are chemically stable, functionalization achieved through this route is generally more durable than that achieved through physical adsorption. A key advantage of chemical surface modification is the creation of robust and long-lasting bioactive sites that significantly improve cell-material interactions, thereby promoting efficient cell adhesion and growth on the nanofiber scaffold [129], [133]. A schematic overview of common surface functionalization strategies for biomedical applications is presented in Fig. 5 [128].

【Wet chemical methods · p1125】Wet-chemical treatment is a widely used functionalization strategy for ESNFs, involving chemical reactions conducted under acidic or basic conditions or in the presence of nucleophiles such as diamines. These reactions typically lead to selective cleavage of polymer chains at labile sites, such as ester bonds commonly present in polyester-based NFs [129]. Unlike purely physical modification methods, which are largely confined to the surface, wet chemical approaches can introduce hydrophilic functional groups both at and beneath the fiber surface, thereby enabling more extensive surface activation. The degree of modification depends on several parameters, including reaction time, reagent type and concentration, and the polymer's intrinsic chemical composition. Careful optimization of these conditions is therefore essential to avoid excessive degradation of the polymer backbone, which may adversely influence the mechanical durability and overall stability of the NFs structure [133], [134]. Through controlled reactions, functional groups such as amine (-NH2), carboxyl (-COOH), and hydroxyl (-OH) can be added onto the nanofiber surface, enhancing its chemical reactivity and suitability for further biofunctionalization. Among the most commonly employed wet chemical approaches are hydrolysis and aminolysis. The efficiency and outcomes of these processes are strongly influenced by reagent type and concentration, as well as exposure duration, all of which govern the degree of surface modification and its compatibility with biomedical applications such as DD and TE [135].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Recent advances in functionalized electrospun nanofibers for biomedical and therapeutic applications: A comprehensive review》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Conclusions · p1805】This review provides an in-depth analysis of recent developments in functionalized ESNFs and their expanding roles across diverse biomedical applications. Emphasis was placed on innovative modification strategies and contemporary techniques to enhance the structural and functional attributes of these nanofibrous scaffolds. Given their unique features, ESNFs demonstrate remarkable appeal across fields such as tissue regeneration, wound healing, targeted DD, and biosensing. Their tunable physicochemical properties and design flexibility further underscore their appeal as multifunctional platforms for both fundamental research and translational biomedical technologies. Nevertheless, fabricating NFs with precisely controlled morphology, superior mechanical and biochemical properties, and high production yield remains a technical challenge. Achieving these goals requires advanced control over the ES process and post-processing functionalization techniques. The use of various functionalization methods, such as plasma treatment, UV irradiation, chemical and biological crosslinking, and LBL deposition, has enabled researchers to tailor the surface chemistry and physico-mechanical properties of NFs to meet specific biomedical requirements. These functionalized NFs can be strategically engineered to direct specific cellular behaviors, including adhesion, proliferation, migration, and differentiation, thereby serving as potent platforms for targeted biomedical interventions. A particularly promising area of application is TE, where NF-based scaffolds are constructed to mimic the architecture and biomechanical characteristics of natural extracellular matrices. These scaffolds support tissue organization in vitro and offer the possibility for in vivo transplantation. ESNFs have also demonstrated potential in facilitating nerve regeneration, bone repair, and VTE and STE. Yet, a key obstacle lies in the tendency of some natural polymer NFs to degrade or lose functional integrity when exposed to physiological conditions, thereby limiting their long-term performance and biocompatibility. As such, identifying novel materials or combining synthetic and natural polymers may offer more reliable alternatives. Despite these advances, significant gaps remain. Most studies to date have used small-animal models, such as rodents, which may not adequately reflect human physiological and immunological conditions. Therefore, validating these findings in larger, clinically relevant animal models is critical before transitioning toward human trials. Furthermore, long-term studies are needed to evaluate the in vivo stability, degradation profiles, immune responses, and therapeutic outcomes of these scaffolds.
